dct_description_sm:
Notes:

The following errors were found:

  • A coding error was discovered in the variable Income status (2000 low income cut-offs) (INCSTP) creating a bias; too many individuals were included in the category "BELOWLINE". The error is now corrected.
  • A coding error was discovered in the variable Ethnic origin (ETHNICRA) affecting two categories: "Not applicable" and "Dutch (Netherlands)". The error is now corrected.
  • A new variable has been added to the file. It is called “Unique record identifier” (PPSORT). Built/included in the file for administrative purposes only.
Appendix B as well as the tools used to measure the quality will not be modified.
Please see target="new">Description of Data Errors For Individuals for more information.

;Notes: In 1991, 1996, and 2001, the Census of Population enumerated both permanent and non-permanent residents of Canada. Non-permanent residents are person from another country who had an employment authorization, a student authorization, or a Minister's permit, or who refugee claimants at the time of census, and family members living with them.
Prior to 1991, only permanent residents of Canada were included in the census. (The only exception to this occured in 1941). Non-permanent residents were considered foreign residents and were not enumerated.;

The 2001 Census Public Use Microdata File (PUMF) on Individuals contains data based on a 2.7% sample of the population enumerated in the census. It provides information on the demographic, social and economic characteristics of the Canadian population. This microdata file allows users to group and manipulate the data to suit their own requirements.

The documentation (metadata) provided in the PUMF on individuals is divided into four chapters: Chapter I contains the record layout, an essential tool for using the file; Chapter II describes the variables included in the file; Chapters III and IV deal with the sampling method and data quality.

Changes in the the 2001 Census:

  • The question on religion, which is asked every 10 years, was re-introduced in 2001.
  • In 2001, two new questions were added: one on the birthplace of parents and the other on the language of work. A second part was also added to the question on home language.
  • In view of the legal recognition of same-sex couples, the census definition of a common-law couple was changed to "two people of the opposite sex or of the same sex who live together as a couple but who are not legally married to each other".
  • The question on fertility was not asked in the 2001 census.
